terms.grammar: adverb, and preposition with the accusative; comparative propius, superlative proximē
evidence: Cic. Fam. 9.7.1: prope alicubī esse (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: As a preposition, with the accusative (prope urbem) or with ab (prope ā meīs aedibus, Cic. Pis. 26). Prope also means “almost” (see almost).

evidence: Cic. Rosc. Am. 133: propinquum praedium (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The adjective; as a noun, a relative (propinquī, one’s relations).
As an adjective mostly poetic (Lewis & Short); as a noun, a neighbour (see neighbour).

terms.grammar: adverb, and preposition with the accusative
evidence: Caes. B.G. 2.26.1: legiō, quae juxtā cōnstiterat (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: cēna brevis juvat et prope rīvum somnus in herbā
phrases.english: I like a light dinner, and a nap in the grass near a stream

phrases.latin: cujus etiam illī hortulī propinquī nōn memoriam sōlum mihi adferunt, sed ipsum videntur in cōnspectū meō pōnere
phrases.english: even his little gardens nearby not only bring him to mind but seem to set the man himself before my eyes
